q: When your teacher is giving a lesson, a good listener should:
o: look at the speaker and wait to ask questions
e: Active listening means paying attention and asking questions.

q: A kindergarten student wants to understand a story better. What should the student do?
o: ask a question about the part that is unclear
e: Asking questions helps you understand information.

q: The teacher says, Put away the blocks, then sit on the rug. What do you do first?
e: Follow oral directions in the order they are given.

q: Restating a direction means:
o: saying it again in your own words
e: Restating shows you understood the direction.

q: Speaking audibly and clearly means that others can:
e: Clear speech is loud enough and easy to understand.

q: Which is the best way to share an idea with the class?
o: stand up and speak in a clear voice
e: Share ideas in a voice that others can hear.

q: In a class discussion, a good rule is to:
o: wait for your turn to talk
e: Taking turns is an agreed-upon discussion rule.

q: When a group works together on a poster, each student should:
o: share the work and listen to the others
e: Collaboration means working with others by the rules.

q: Which is a polite way to start a conversation with a new classmate?
o: say hello and tell your name
e: Introductions and greetings build social communication.

q: When a visitor enters the room in the morning, a student can say:
e: Buenos días is a morning greeting.

q: Before writing a story, a student can plan by:
e: Planning can start with talk and drawings.

q: Planning a piece of writing means:
o: getting ideas ready before you write
e: Planning generates ideas for writing.

q: A draft is a first try at writing that you:
o: can later change and make better
e: Drafts organize ideas and can be revised.

q: A kindergartner can make a draft by:
o: drawing a picture or writing words about an idea
e: Drafts may be oral, pictorial or written.

q: To revise a drawing for your story, you might:
o: add more details to the picture
e: Revising adds details in pictures or words.

q: Revising means:
o: making your work better by adding details
e: Revising improves a draft.

q: A complete sentence always tells:
o: who or what and what happens
e: A sentence has a subject and an action.

q: Ser and estar both mean to be. Which sentence uses estar to tell where something is?
o: La mesa está en la sala.
e: Estar tells location or a changing condition.

q: Which sentence uses ser to tell what someone is like?
e: Ser tells identity and lasting traits.

q: Which article goes with the feminine word casa?
e: Casa is feminine, so it uses la.

q: What is the plural of the word libro?
e: Add s to a noun that ends in a vowel.

q: Which phrase has an article and an adjective that agree?
e: Articles and adjectives agree with the noun.

q: An adjective is a word that:
e: Adjectives tell more about nouns.

q: In Spanish, the letter h at the start of a word is usually:
e: Silent h is a spelling pattern in Spanish.

q: Which word is a preposition that tells where?
e: Prepositions show position or relationship.

q: In the sentence El libro está en la mesa, the word en tells:
e: En is a preposition showing place.

q: Which pronoun is formal, used to address an adult politely?
e: Usted is the formal you.

q: A kindergartner speaks to a friend. The informal pronoun is:
e: Tú is the informal you for a friend.

q: A sentence should begin with:
e: Capitalize the first letter of a sentence.

q: The name of a person begins with:
e: Names begin with a capital letter.

q: A sentence that tells something ends with:
e: A declarative sentence ends with a period.

q: Which sentence has the correct end mark?
e: Telling sentences end with a period.

q: When you finish writing, you can:
e: Writers share their work.

q: Sharing your writing means:
o: letting others read or hear it
e: Sharing gives writing an audience.

q: A personal narrative is a story about:
e: Personal narratives tell about your own experiences.

q: A kindergartner who cannot write yet can compose a story by:
o: telling it to an adult who writes it down
e: Dictation is a way to compose.

q: An informational text tries to:
e: Informational texts give facts.

q: Which sentence could be in an informational text?
e: Informational writing gives true facts.

q: A question you ask to learn about frogs is part of:
e: Inquiry starts with questions.

q: With an adult, which is a good question to research?
e: Good research questions ask about a topic.

q: A research plan tells:
o: the steps you will take to find answers
e: A plan lists how you will find information.

q: With help, a class makes a research plan before:
e: Plan first, then research.

q: To find out about bees, you can gather information from:
o: books and videos with an adult
e: Use a variety of sources.

q: A source is:
e: Books and videos are sources.

q: After you gather facts about bees, you show you understand by:
e: Understanding means you can explain information.

q: Which shows understanding of what you read?
o: saying a fact in your own words
e: Restating shows understanding.

q: To share what you learned, you can present results by:
e: Delivery may be written, oral or multimodal.

q: Presenting results in a multimodal way uses:
o: words together with pictures or sound
e: Multimodal means more than one mode.

q: Which two words rhyme?
e: Rhyming words end with the same sound.

q: Say a word that rhymes with mesa. A good choice is:
e: Mesa and pesa end with the same sound.

q: Which words start with the same sound?
e: Alliteration means words begin with the same sound.

q: Which set begins with the same simple syllable?
e: They all begin with ma.

q: How many words are in the spoken sentence Yo veo un gato?
e: Count each word: yo, veo, un, gato.

q: The sentence La niña canta has how many words?
e: The words are la, niña, canta.

q: How many syllables are in the word mesa?
e: Me-sa has two syllables.

q: How many syllables do you hear in the word mariposa?
e: Ma-ri-po-sa has four syllables.

q: Take the syllable ca out of casa. What is left?
e: Deleting a syllable leaves the rest of the word.

q: Change the first syllable of mesa to pe. What is the new word?
e: Replacing the first syllable creates a new word.

q: Blend the syllables ga and to. What word do you make?
e: Blending joins syllables into a word.

q: Which word do you get by putting ma and no together?
e: Ma plus no makes mano.

q: Say the word luna one syllable at a time. What are the parts?
e: Luna splits into lu-na.

q: Clap the syllables of pelota. How many claps?
e: Pe-lo-ta has three syllables.

q: What is the first sound in the word sol?
e: The first sound in sol is s.

q: What is the last sound in the word pan?
e: Pan ends with the sound n.

q: Blend the sounds m and a. What syllable do you make?
e: M plus a blends to ma.

q: Blend the sounds s and o. What syllable do you make?
e: S plus o blends to so.

q: Which letter makes the sound at the start of the word luna?
e: The first letter of luna is l.

q: The letter m stands for the sound at the beginning of:
e: Mesa begins with m.

q: Use letter sounds to read this word: sapo. What are its syllables?
e: Decode one syllable at a time.

q: Which word is made from the syllables ca and ma?
e: Ca plus ma reads cama.

q: In the Spanish word hola, the letter h:
e: H is silent in Spanish.

q: Which word has the digraph ll?
e: The letters ll form one digraph.

q: If you change the last syllable of mesa from sa to ta, you get:
e: Changing a syllable makes a new word.

q: Adding the syllable ca to the front of sa makes:
e: Adding a syllable creates a new word.

q: Which letter should you use to spell the first sound in sapo?
e: Spelling matches sounds to letters.

q: The sound you hear at the end of the word pan is spelled with:
e: Pan ends with n.

q: Which word follows the CV pattern for each of its two syllables?
e: Me and sa are each consonant plus vowel.

q: The word sol follows which syllable pattern?
e: Consonant, vowel, consonant.

q: Which part of a book has the title and picture on the outside?
e: The front cover shows the title.

q: The title page is found:
o: inside the book near the beginning
e: The title page names the book inside.

q: When you read a book, you hold it:
e: Hold the book right side up.

q: In Spanish and English books, reading moves:
o: from left to right and top to bottom
e: Text is read left to right, top to bottom.

q: In the sentence Yo amo mi casa, how many spaces are between words?
e: Four words have three spaces between them.

q: A single letter and a printed word are different because a word:
e: A word is a group of letters.

q: Which of these is a letter, not a word?
e: One mark is a letter.

q: Which letter is the uppercase form of the letter a?
e: Uppercase A matches lowercase a.

q: The lowercase partner of the letter M is:
e: Uppercase M goes with lowercase m.

q: When you write a letter, you should form it:
o: starting at the right place and moving in the right direction
e: Handwriting uses correct strokes and direction.

q: A good handwriting habit for kindergartners is to:
e: Letters sit on the baseline.

q: A picture dictionary helps you to:
o: find a word and see its picture
e: A picture dictionary shows words with pictures.

q: To find a word you do not know, you can look in:
e: Dictionaries help find words.

q: A picture in a story can help you learn:
e: Illustrations help clarify word meanings.

q: When you hear an unfamiliar word in a read-aloud, you can:
o: look at the pictures for a clue
e: Use illustrations to learn word meanings.

q: Which word is an action word?
e: Action words tell what someone does.

q: Which word names a position?
e: Position words tell where something is.

q: Listening, speaking, reading and writing are all:
o: language skills that help each other grow
e: Foundational language skills are developed together.

q: When students listen to a story and then talk about it, they are using:
e: Language skills work together.

q: Why do we read a story?
o: to enjoy it or to learn something
e: Readers have a purpose for reading.

q: Before you read a book, you can set a purpose by asking:
o: What do I want to learn?
e: A purpose guides reading.

q: Asking questions before, during and after reading helps you:
e: Questions build understanding.

q: Which is a good question to ask during reading?
o: Why did the character do that?
e: Questions about the text help understanding.

q: Looking at the cover and guessing what will happen is called:
e: Predictions use text features.

q: After you read, you confirm a prediction by checking:
e: Confirm predictions against the text.

q: Creating a picture in your mind while a story is read is called:
e: Mental images deepen understanding.

q: If a story says the sun is bright over a green hill, you can picture:
e: Words help the reader visualize.

q: Saying This story reminds me of my dog is making:
e: Connections link text to experience.

q: A story about a birthday makes you think of your own party. This is a:
e: Personal connections tie text to your life.

q: An inference is when you:
o: use clues to figure out something not said
e: Inferences use evidence.

q: A girl wears a coat and mittens. What can you infer?
e: Clues in the text support inferences.

q: Deciding which details are most important in a story means you:
e: Evaluating details finds what matters most.

q: Which detail is most important in a story about a lost puppy?
e: The main problem is the key detail.

q: Putting together ideas from a text to make a new understanding is:
e: Synthesis creates new understanding.

q: After reading two books about frogs, you combine what you learned. This is called:
e: Synthesis combines information.

q: If a sentence does not make sense, you can fix your understanding by:
e: Re-reading is a comprehension strategy.

q: Monitoring comprehension means:
o: checking whether you understand as you read
e: Readers check and adjust their understanding.

q: A personal connection to a text is when you:
o: tell how it relates to your own life
e: Personal connections are a response to text.

q: After a story about friends, you say I have a friend like that. This is a:
e: Describing personal connections is a response.

q: After reading, you can respond by:
e: Responses may be oral, pictorial or written.

q: One way to respond to a story is to:
e: A drawing is a pictorial response.

q: Text evidence is:
o: something in the text that supports your answer
e: Evidence comes from the text.

q: You say the boy was sad because he cried. The word cried is:
e: Evidence supports the response.

q: To retell a story, you:
e: Retelling keeps the meaning.

q: A good retelling includes the beginning, the middle and:
e: A retelling follows story order.

q: One meaningful way to interact with a book is to:
e: Illustrating and writing are responses.

q: After reading, you can show what you know by:
o: drawing a picture of the story
e: Interacting with sources shows understanding.

q: Using a new word you just learned when you talk about a book shows:
o: you can respond with new vocabulary
e: Use newly acquired vocabulary in responses.

q: The teacher teaches the word brillante. A student says, El sol es brillante. This shows:
e: Using new vocabulary in response.

q: The theme of a story is:
o: the big idea the story is about
e: Theme is the basic idea or message.

q: A story shows friends sharing and helping. A possible theme is:
e: Text evidence points to the theme.

q: The main character is:
o: the most important character in the story
e: The main character is who the story is about.

q: A story is mostly about a boy who plants a garden. The main character is:
e: The main character is who the story is mostly about.

q: The problem in a story is the:
e: Plot includes problem and resolution.

q: The resolution of a story tells:
e: The resolution solves the problem.

q: The setting of a story is:
e: Setting is place and time.

q: A story takes place at a beach in summer. The beach is part of the:
e: The beach tells where the story happens.

q: Which is a well-known children's story type with talking animals and a lesson?
e: Fables are short stories with a lesson.

q: A fairy tale often begins with:
e: Fairy tales often use a traditional opening.

q: In a nursery poem, words that end with the same sound make:
e: Rhyme is repeated ending sounds.

q: The beat you feel when you clap along to a poem is its:
e: Rhythm is the beat of a poem.

q: In a play, the main characters are the ones who:
e: Main characters in drama carry the action.

q: A drama is a story that is meant to be:
e: Drama is acted out.

q: The central idea of an informational text is:
o: what the text is mostly about
e: Central idea is the main point.

q: A book about bees tells how they make honey and live in hives. The central idea is:
e: Supporting details point to the central idea.

q: A title helps you know:
e: Titles give information.

q: A simple graphic such as a diagram of a plant can:
e: Graphics add information.

q: Steps in a sequence are told:
e: Sequence follows order.

q: Words like first, then and last help show:
e: Sequence words organize steps.

q: Persuasive text tries to:
o: convince you to think or do something
e: Persuasive text has an author's goal.

q: An author writes, You should read every day because it helps you learn. The author wants you to:
e: The author is trying to persuade.

q: A digital text is one that you read:
e: Digital texts appear on screens.

q: A multimodal text combines words with:
e: Multimodal texts use more than one mode.

q: An author's purpose is:
o: the reason the author wrote the text
e: Authors write to inform, entertain or persuade.

q: A funny story about a silly dog was probably written to:
e: The purpose is to entertain.

q: Text structure means:
o: how the author organizes the writing
e: Structure shows how ideas are organized.

q: An author puts steps in order to show how to make a sandwich. This structure is:
e: Sequence helps the author's purpose.

q: Bold words and pictures in a book are:
e: Features highlight information.

q: An author uses a bold heading to:
e: Headings organize information.

q: Words that help you picture a scene are:
e: Describing words help readers visualize.

q: An author writes the red ball bounced high. These words help you:
e: Imagery supports visualizing.

q: A story told by someone who says I is in:
e: First-person text uses I.

q: A story told with the words he and she about other people is in:
e: Third person tells about others.
